doc.title: Jerry Gordon interviewed by Monk Rowe and Christian Goodwillie, via Zoom, June 30, 2021

chapter: Selling the store and founding Evidence
title: What independent labels are independent of
summary: Gordon explains majors versus indies and says starting Evidence was like opening the store, a leap he never doubted.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Okay. Let’s move on, it’s really fascinating stuff. I want to move on to Evidence Records. And this seems like an obvious question but we often read about the Indies, the small record labels. I don’t know if most people including myself know what exactly does that mean? If you’re an independent record label owner, what are you independent of?

You were independent of the quote majors unquote. So in my days at Third Street Jazz you had many majors who were, they were RCA, and those who they distributed or other labels that they owned. There was Warner Brothers which included Electra; and Atlantic. There was, you know, Columbia and Epic. So there were like let’s say seven majors. Right — there had been a consolidation right before I opened my record store when Electra was an Indy label. Atlantic was an Indy label. Okay? Because they were not a part of these conglomerates. So let’s say there were seven conglomerates in the 70s and early 80s okay? I think now there’s three. Okay? I mean the record business has continued to consolidate in that way. So while, so at Third Street I remember the first album, the first album on Alligator coming out. I remember the first album on Sunnyside coming out. You know, these are labels that have grown and are revered and they were never owned by operated by or engulfed by one of these larger corporations. Those are the Indies.

So you can say the same thing about Evidence that you weren’t having to report up the chain. You were at the top of the chain, you and your partner, and again I’ll ask the same question about — I asked about the record store — did you go into this with confidence that it could sustain itself?

I wouldn’t have done it if I didn’t think so. But opening my store it was okay — what’s my rent, what do the records cost, what can you sell them for, how many do I have to sell to meet my rent — okay, here I go, boom. It’s like walking off a cliff and you either are, you know you’re going to fly or you’re going to sink, and I never considered sinking, I couldn’t afford it.
